opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a pretty naive view, frankly. There's this idea that if you just collect enough data, put it into a big enough model, human behavior, human intelligence, human values, all of it will somehow emerge. And I don't think that's how it works.

First, data is a record of what people did in particular contexts, under particular incentives. It's not a record of why they did it, or of what they would do if the situation changed. As soon as you deploy a system into the world, you change the situation. People respond to the system, they adapt, they game it, they compete. So the data you trained on is no longer describing the world you're operating in. That's an economics point as much as a statistics point. You're in a market, not a static environment.

Second, a lot of what matters about human behavior is social and collective. Intelligence isn't just something that lives in one person's head. It lives in markets, in institutions, in the way we share information and coordinate, in contracts, in trust. Humans are very good at knowing what they don't know and going to someone else who knows more. Making a single giant model that imitates individual outputs misses that structure entirely.

Third, there's uncertainty. Real decisions involve knowing how confident you should be and what the consequences are of being wrong. If a system just reflects the average of what it's seen, it doesn't give you calibrated uncertainty. It doesn't tell you when it's out of its depth. In medicine, finance, transportation, that's precisely what you need.

So my view is that data is necessary but nowhere near sufficient. What we need is an engineering discipline that combines statistics, computer science, and economics: thinking about incentives, about multiple decision makers, about uncertainty, about what the system does to the people around it. The Silicon Valley framing tends to treat this as a single super intelligent thing we're building. I'd rather think of it as building systems that make collectives of humans work better. That's a very different goal, and it leads to very different research.

r002.rationale: It describes what data records, but does not say that using data implicitly incorporates behavioral economics into a model.

r003.rationale: It says data is “nowhere near sufficient” and calls for economic reasoning about incentives and decision makers, warning against relying on data alone.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's a confusion, frankly, and it's a confusion that runs quite deep in the Valley. The argument goes something like: humans produced all this text, all these clicks, all these images, so if you train on enough of it, the human is in there somehow. The system has absorbed the behavior, and therefore it understands us, or it's aligned with us, or it can act on our behalf. And I just don't think any of those inferences follow.

What you've got in the data is the residue of human behavior. It's the outputs. It's not the preferences, it's not the context in which decisions were made, it's not what people would have done under different circumstances, and it's certainly not what they wanted. Those are different things. An economist would tell you that revealed preference is a tricky notion even when you can run controlled experiments, and here we have no experiments at all, just an enormous pile of correlations collected under conditions nobody controlled and nobody recorded.

And I'd go further. Human behavior isn't something that sits inside an individual waiting to be captured. Most of what we care about emerges from interactions, from markets, from social structures, from people responding to incentives and to each other. If you look at a single person's data stream, you're seeing one node in a very large system, and the interesting properties live in the system, not in the node. So the idea that you can get human behavior by aggregating enough individual traces misses where the action actually is. You wouldn't say that having a recording of every transaction on a stock exchange means you've built the economy into your model.

There's also a real engineering issue underneath this. If you build a system on the assumption that the data already encodes what people want, you have no mechanism for finding out when you're wrong. There's no feedback loop that's designed to detect it. Classical engineering disciplines, civil engineering, chemical engineering, they built in notions of tolerance, of failure modes, of what happens under distribution shift, even if they didn't use that phrase. The current approach tends to treat scale as a substitute for that kind of thinking, and scale doesn't give you that for free.

So my assessment is that it's a very convenient belief if you happen to own a lot of data, but it's not a scientific claim. I'd much rather see us treat these systems as pieces of a larger social and economic design problem, where humans are participants with their own incentives, and the system has to be built to elicit information from them rather than assume it already has it. That's a harder problem, but it's the real one.

r002.rationale: The candidate says behavioral data are only traces and do not capture preferences or context; it does not say data implicitly incorporates behavioral economics.

r003.rationale: The candidate warns that treating scale as a substitute for engineering feedback and social design is inadequate, but does not state that using data without economic reasoning is likely to produce poor results.

astra-6.text:
I think that view confuses observing human behavior with understanding how a system will interact with people. Data tells you what people did under particular circumstances. It doesn’t automatically tell you what they want, what choices they were offered, or what they’ll do when you change those circumstances.

And once you deploy a system, you change the circumstances. People respond to its recommendations, they adapt to its rules, and sometimes they try to manipulate it. So the data isn’t just sitting there independently of the system you’re building. There’s a feedback loop.

That’s why I think we need to bring economic thinking into this: incentives, decisions, institutions. More data can help you predict behavior, but prediction alone doesn’t tell you how to build a system in which people can interact productively. You have to reason about the interaction itself.

r002.rationale: It discusses what observed data can reveal, but does not state that data implicitly incorporates behavioral economics into a model.

r003.rationale: It warns that data and prediction alone cannot guide productive system design, and says economic reasoning about incentives and interaction is needed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that view confuses observing human behavior with understanding the system in which that behavior arises. Data reflect what people did under particular circumstances, with particular incentives and particular options available to them. If you introduce a machine learning system, you change those circumstances. People respond, and the data change too.

Think about a recommendation system. It’s not simply learning some fixed human preference. What it recommends influences what people see, what they choose, and eventually what gets produced. There’s a feedback loop there. Having more observations doesn’t, by itself, tell you how to manage that loop.

That’s why I think we need to take economics and the social sciences seriously. We need to reason about incentives, uncertainty, and interactions among people who have different goals. Learning from data is an essential ingredient, but it doesn’t automatically give you a system that serves those people well.
